statement.p:
Suppose that A is a 2\times2 matrix having eigenvectors \vvec_1 and \vvec_2 with associated eigenvalues \lambda_1=3 and \lambda_2 = -6. Because the eigenvalues are real and distinct, we know
that these eigenvectors form a basis of \real^2.
What are the products A\vvec_1 and A\vvec_2 in terms of \vvec_1 and \vvec_2?
If we form the matrix P = \begin{bmatrix} \vvec_1 \amp \vvec_2 \end{bmatrix} , what is the product AP in terms of \vvec_1 and \vvec_2?
Use the eigenvalues to form the diagonal matrix D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp -6 \end{bmatrix} and determine the product PD in terms of \vvec_1 and \vvec_2.
The results from the previous two parts of this activity demonstrate that AP=PD. Using the fact that the eigenvectors \vvec_1 and \vvec_2 form a basis of \real^2, explain why P is invertible and that we must have A=PDP^{-1}.
Suppose that A=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \amp 6 \\ 3 \amp 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}. Verify that \vvec_1=\twovec11 and \vvec_2=\twovec2{-1} are eigenvectors of A with eigenvalues \lambda_1 = 3 and \lambda_2=-6.
Use the Sage cell below to define the matrices P and D and then verify that A=PDP^{-1}.
# enter the matrices P and D below P = D = P*D*P.inverse()

li.p: Since the eigenvectors form a basis, the columns of P are linearly independent and their span is \real^2. This guarantees that P is invertible. Multiplying the equation AP=PD on the right by P^{-1} gives APP^{-1} = A = PDP^{-1}.
